title: Trembling and astonishment (Mark 16:1–8)
hookLine: the women find the tomb empty; the oldest copies end with them fleeing, afraid

lines: VERY EARLY, THE FIRST DAY OF THE WEEK.
WHO WILL ROLL AWAY THE STONE?
cards: The Sabbath is over. Very early on Sunday, as the sun comes up, three women walk to the tomb: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome.
They've bought spices to anoint his body, the last thing they can do for him. On the way they worry about something very practical: who will roll away the stone for us? Mark says it was very great.
Two of them had seen where he was laid. Then they look up. The stone is already rolled back.

teach.h: A YOUNG MAN IN A WHITE ROBE.
teach.b: They go into the tomb, and sitting on the right side is a young man in a long white robe. They are terrified.
He says, in the King James Bible: "Be not affrighted: Ye seek Jesus of Nazareth, which was crucified: he is risen; he is not here: behold the place where they laid him."

Then a message: go, tell his disciples, and Peter, that he goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he said. And Peter. Of all the names to single out, the one who denied him three times by the fire.

Then comes the last verse of Mark in the oldest complete copies: "And they went out quickly, and fled from the sepulchre; for they trembled and were amazed: neither said they any thing to any man; for they were afraid."
That's it. No appearance of the risen Jesus. No reunion.
Just women running from an empty tomb, shaking.
In Greek the sentence ends, literally, they were afraid, for: on a small word, gar, like a sentence cut off mid-breath. Scholars still argue about it. Maybe the last page was lost.

teach.h: HE IS RISEN; HE IS NOT HERE.
teach.b: Maybe Mark meant to stop here. If he did, the ending is a kind of invitation: the story isn't finished; it hands the next step to whoever is reading.
And the women can't have stayed silent forever, or there'd be no story to read. Mark leaves them in trembling and astonishment: not calm, not neat, but awe.
Trembling is tromos; astonishment is ekstasis, a word for being beside yourself, something so big it takes a person outside themselves.

how: Christians celebrate the resurrection at Easter and on Sundays; some churches hold sunrise services on Easter morning, and Orthodox Christians greet each other with Christ is risen, answered, truly he is risen.

o: a quiet joy that settles a troubled heart
astonishment so great you're beside yourself
the trembling that comes with deep fear

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: who will roll away the stone?
he is risen; he is not here
the one singled out by name

s: the oldest copies of Mark end with the women afraid
in Mark 16:1–8 the risen Jesus appears to the women
a young man gives them a message; Jesus himself doesn't appear in these verses.
the young man names Peter specially

games.q: you've found the stone rolled back and a young man tells you: he is risen, go and tell. what do the women do, in Mark's oldest ending?
o: run and tell everyone at once.
flee, trembling, and say nothing, for they were afraid.
stay and wait at the tomb.
games.why: they fled, trembling and astonished, and said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid. that's where the oldest copies end.

practice: Think of something in your life that ended, a job, a friendship, a season, a home, and remember what the women carried on that walk: the heaviness, the practical worries, who will roll away the stone.
Then ask gently what began after that ending, even if you didn't see it at the time; you don't need a neat answer. If you pray, you can hold that ending before God.
